I'm looking at a proposal from another AI that outlines a major technical overhaul for Vera—moving to Vite, removing CDN dependencies, switching to CSS Modules or CSS-in-JS, and migrating to Supabase with PostgreSQL and row-level security. I need to give Juanfra a realistic assessment of this roadmap based on what we've actually discovered about the codebase today.

Starting with the bundler migration: this would be an enormous undertaking. Vera's currently a single-file `src/app.jsx` compiled via esbuild in Docker and deployed with rsync and docker-compose. Moving to Vite would require completely rearchitecting the build pipeline and splitting that monolithic file into modules—a massive refactor risk given how tightly coupled everything is. We've seen today how even small isolated changes caused real production incidents, so a full bundler migration could easily take weeks and introduce numerous regressions. And honestly, for a small-scale wedding CRM serving just a handful of studios, load speed probably isn't the actual bottleneck limiting growth.

The CDN dependency removal is actually reasonable and lower-risk—installing npm packages locally instead of loading React, jsPDF, and QR code libraries from unpkg or jsdelivr. This doesn't require Vite at all; it can work within the existing esbuild setup. It's a legitimate concern since external CDN uptime is a real reliability risk, so this piece of advice actually makes sense without the whole migration.

CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS similarly assume a modular multi-file component structure that doesn't exist yet. Since everything's in one giant file, "CSS Modules per component" doesn't naturally fit unless the JavaScript itself gets modularized too—which brings us back to the bundler migration and its disproportionate risk.

Migrating to Postgres with RLS is a massive undertaking that would require completely rewriting the data access layer and re-verifying every query we've audited today. Given how much work went into confirming tenant isolation and preventing cross-studio data leaks, moving to RLS would mean redoing all that verification from scratch with real risk of missing a policy and causing the exact data leak we spent effort preventing. It's worth considering long-term but not something to rush into.

I should push back on the framing here—this reads like generic best practices advice disconnected from Vera's actual situation: single developer, single VPS, handful of real customers, and we've been iterating fast with users already live. The real bottleneck we've spent the whole session on wasn't infrastructure but product bugs and reliability issues in the CRM domain logic. A wholesale rewrite risks weeks of instability for infrastructure gains that may not even matter to growth right now. I should acknowledge what's legitimately useful (removing CDN dependencies is a reasonable low-risk win) while pushing back hard on the Vite migration and CSS-in-JS as premature and disproportionately risky given Vera's scale and how many subtle bugs we've found from much smaller changes.

The database migration to Postgres or Supabase is also premature—SQLite via node:sqlite has been working fine, and switching databases risks reintroducing exactly the kind of tenant-isolation bugs we spent real effort verifying today with cross-studio penetration testing. That would need RLS implemented from scratch. The actual bottleneck for MVP launch, based on what we've learned today, is correctness and reliability of the domain logic and processes—things like retroactive email fires on rule creation, contaminated test data leaking into production, timezone bugs, silent data corruption, and cross-tenant leaks if not carefully checked. That's where the real risk lies, not the framework or infrastructure choices.

I should be direct here: don't do the infrastructure rewrite now. The real differentiators for competitiveness are reliability and trust—no more test data bleeding into production, no more automations firing incorrectly. Everything else is premature and risks reintroducing the exact regressions we've spent all session carefully avoiding.…Voy a ser honesto, porque esto se lee como una hoja de ruta genérica de buenas prácticas, no como algo calibrado al estado real de Vera ni a lo que hemos visto hoy con nuestras propias manos. Vamos punto por punto.

**Lo único que me parece razonable de los cuatro puntos: quitar las dependencias de CDN.** Cargar React/jsPDF/QR desde `unpkg`/`jsdelivr` sí es un riesgo real y evitable — si ese servidor externo tiene un mal día, tu app deja de cargar sin que tú hayas tocado nada. Y esto se puede hacer **sin** migrar a Vite: `npm install` las dependencias y que esbuild (que ya tienes funcionando) las empaquete localmente. Bajo riesgo, beneficio real. **El resto — Vite, CSS Modules, y sobre todo migrar de SQLite a Supabase/Postgres — lo desaconsejo firmemente ahora mismo, y no por dogma, sino por lo que hemos visto hoy con datos reales:**

Llevamos una sesión entera encontrando bugs sutiles en cambios mucho más pequeños que una migración de framework o de base de datos — el `mousedown` que roba el foco antes del `click`, el `e.target.value` leído después de que se reseteara, `new Date()` interpretando una zona horaria equivocada, un `useMemo` con un array de dependencias incompleto. Estos son bugs de una línea, en un proyecto que conocemos al detalle. Una migración de Vite significa reestructurar `src/app.jsx` entero en módulos — el mismo archivo donde hoy conviven docenas de funciones compartidas que hemos ido descubriendo y arreglando una a una (`weddingRecipientEmail`, `sendQueuedEmail`, `findRetroactiveMatches`...). Y la migración de base de datos es más seria todavía. Hoy hemos pasado un tiempo real verificando, con pruebas de penetración entre estudios reales, que ningún estudio puede ver los datos de otro (`sub.user_id !== req.userId`, comprobado explícitamente con dos cuentas de prueba). ### 🤖 Claude

I'm thinking through how the automation actually prevents duplicate sends when a lead responds before the scheduled email fires. The key is understanding what happens during the daily scan—when checking if a lead still meets the `lead_sin_respuesta` condition, the system needs to verify the lead is still in the `stage='lead'` state and hasn't received a response within the X-day window, so if they've already responded, they'd no longer qualify for that automation trigger. 't trigger at all. The test case with Lead B already proved this — once the stage changed, the automation skipped them even though days had passed. So the real answer is simpler: Juanfra just needs to update the lead's stage when they respond, and the daily scan will automatically exclude them from future sends because they no longer meet the trigger condition. No manual cancellation needed, and the system is already designed to handle this correctly.

But there's a practical timing risk I should mention: if a lead responds on day 3 but Juanfra doesn't update their stage in Vera until day 6, the automation could still fire on day 5 while the stage is still showing as "lead" in the CRM. The system can only work with what's actually recorded in the database, not what happened in the real world. So the mechanism protects him as long as he updates the stage promptly when they respond — that's the key habit that makes this work reliably.

I think the best approach is to explain how the existing stage-based mechanism already handles this (and point to the Lead B test as proof), clarify the practical dependency on timely stage updates, and then offer an optional enhancement: an explicit "don't send this" button per rule that acts as an independent safety net, similar to how "Enviar ahora" works as an override.…Buena pregunta, y la respuesta es tranquilizadora: **el mecanismo ya está diseñado para resolver exactamente esto, sin que tengas que hacer nada especial — solo con lo que ya harías de todas formas.**

La condición del disparador no es "han pasado 5 días desde que entró el lead" a secas — es "**sigue en la etapa 'Lead' sin avanzar**, 5 días después". Eso significa: si ese lead te contesta el día 3 y tú lo mueves de etapa en el pipeline (a "Contactado", "Reunión agendada", o lo que sea el siguiente paso), el día 5, cuando corra el escaneo, ese lead **ya no cumple la condición** — no está en la etapa "Lead" sin avanzar — y el sistema no le envía nada, automáticamente. Esto no es una suposición: es literalmente lo que se acaba de verificar hace un momento con datos reales ("Lead B", que avanzó de etapa, no disparó aunque tenía más de 3 días).

Así que el "cómo lo anulo" es, en la práctica: **muévelo de etapa en cuanto te conteste**, algo que probablemente ya haces para llevar tu pipeline al día. No hace falta ningún botón de "cancelar" aparte.

**Lo único que tienes que tener en cuenta:** el sistema solo sabe lo que tú le dices en el CRM. Si el lead te contesta el día 3 pero tú no actualizas su etapa hasta el día 6 (por estar liado, por ejemplo), y el escaneo corrió el día 5 con el lead todavía marcado como "Lead" en el sistema, sí le llegaría el email — porque, desde el punto de vista de Vera, en ese momento seguía sin respuesta. La fiabilidad de esto depende de que actualices la etapa con relativa rapidez cuando te contesten, no de que exista un mecanismo mágico que detecte respuestas de email automáticamente (eso no existe hoy en Vera).

Si quieres una capa extra de seguridad —un botón explícito "No enviar esto a esta boda" independiente de mover la etapa, para los casos en que sepas que no vas a poder actualizar el pipeline a tiempo—, lo puedo preparar como brief aparte. ¿Te interesa, o con mover la etapa a tiempo te vale?

The tool-level issues have reportedly been patched across several versions and mainly matter for Juanfra's own machine security, not Vera's application security. Far more directly relevant is the second category — security patterns in AI-generated code itself. The Alberto Pampín blog source is very concrete here: without security instructions, Claude tends to generate CRM code with IDOR flaws, SQL injection via concatenated search terms, MD5-hashed passwords, and unrestricted CSV imports. Since Vera is literally a CRM, this maps directly onto the exact class of bugs I should be auditing for.

## 1. Vulnerabilidades de la propia herramienta Claude Code (no de Vera)

Sí, ha habido vulnerabilidades reales y documentadas en Claude Code como aplicación — un bypass de sandbox de red, ejecución remota de código al abrir un repositorio no confiable con configuración maliciosa, y una fuga de la clave API vía manipulación de `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. Todas están **ya corregidas** (versiones 1.0.87, 1.0.111, 2.0.65 y 2.1.90 respectivamente, la más reciente de mayo de 2026). Esto es un riesgo para **tu propio ordenador y tus credenciales** mientras usas la herramienta (por ejemplo, si alguna vez clonas un repositorio de origen dudoso), pero no significa que el código que ha generado para Vera tenga esas vulnerabilidades — son cosas distintas.

## 2. Patrones de fallo típicos en código generado por IA sin instrucciones de seguridad — esto sí es directamente relevante para Vera

Encontré algo muy concreto y útil: un análisis describe exactamente qué falla por defecto cuando se le pide a una IA que construya un CRM sin instrucciones de seguridad explícitas — y es casi una descripción literal de lo que deberíamos auditar en Vera:

- **Fallo IDOR** (acceso a datos de otro usuario cambiando un ID en la URL, sin comprobar que pertenece a tu cuenta)
- **Inyección SQL** por concatenar términos de búsqueda directamente en la consulta
- **Contraseñas con hash débil** (MD5 en vez de algo robusto)
- **Importaciones sin límite de tamaño**

Esto es oro para nosotros porque ya sabemos que Vera **sí ha pasado** al menos una prueba de este tipo — recuerda la verificación cruzada entre dos estudios reales que hicimos hace tiempo para `form_submissions` (404, no 200, al intentar acceder a datos de otro estudio). Pero eso fue **un solo endpoint probado explícitamente** — no hay garantía de que **todos** los demás (bodas, plantillas, formularios, contratos, facturas) tengan la misma comprobación.

Voy a construir un plan de auditoría real basado en estos 4 patrones concretos, aplicado sistemáticamente a Vera — no una promesa vaga de "vamos a revisar seguridad", sino una lista verificable con pruebas reales, igual que hemos hecho con todo lo demás hoy.

### 🤖 Claude

Since I couldn't get whisper models downloaded, the user provided the transcript directly, so now I'm digging into what's actually applicable to Vera. The core issue described is regression risk in AI-built apps: as features get added via Claude, ChatGPT, or Lovable, something that worked for months can silently break, and developers often learn about it from the client instead of catching it themselves.

The proposed fix combines Playwright for web end-to-end testing, verification of actual computed results on mobile (not just visual correctness — wrong calorie calculations in a nutrition app could be genuinely harmful, not just annoying), and GitHub Actions CI to automatically run tests on every change and block deploys if anything fails.

This maps directly onto our entire session — every verification we've done has been manual, with disposable test accounts, clicking through the UI or hitting the API, checking the database, and cleaning up afterward. That's exactly the fragile, non-automated pattern this solution is meant to replace.

The risk is real: every time a shared function like `weddingRecipientEmail`, `sendQueuedEmail`, `findRetroactiveMatches`, `plainBodyToHtml`, or `computeAutoName` gets touched, we're relying entirely on Code (or me, drafting the brief) remembering to imagine every place that could regress. We already saw this fail once — the wizard's name field had a stale bug that only surfaced because Juanfra happened to notice it in the UI, not because any systematic test caught it.

This maps exactly to the audio's core lesson — the bigger Vera gets, the more surface area there is to quietly break something without noticing, and today alone Vera grew massively (automation engine, form builder, real-time notifications, four trigger types). Manual testing has worked because of exceptional discipline, but it doesn't scale, and the failure mode is precisely what the audio describes: something quietly breaks and Juanfra's real clients find out before anyone at Vera does.

The audio also gives me a concrete path forward — for the web app, a Playwright E2E suite walking through key user journeys like login, creating a lead, creating a wedding, sending a form, signing a contract, and completing an automation trigger.

I'm also thinking about correctness of internal calculations rather than just surface-level "looks fine" — things like the date math for automation triggers, the price/package computation, the automatic name generator, the retroactive-match counting logic, and the email fallback function are exactly the kind of quiet-but-wrong bugs I've spent all day hunting one at a time, and unit tests for these pure functions would catch regressions automatically instead of relying on memory. And the biggest structural gap right now is CI — running the test suite automatically on every push to main and blocking deploy on failure, since currently every deploy happens without that safety net.

Right now, deploys go straight to the VPS via rsync and a docker-compose rebuild with no gate except a session's own manual verification, meaning a future change that breaks something outside that session's manual tests would reach real photographers and clients with zero safety net. This is a bigger infrastructure request than the feature/bug-fix work we've done today, so I need to scope it carefully—starting with discovery of which functions failed most, then designing a testing setup that fits Vera's existing rsync/docker-compose deploy flow without disrupting it.

Deploy right now is entirely manual, Code runs rsync then docker-compose up -d --build by hand, no existing CI/CD. So "GitHub Action blocks deploy" doesn't map cleanly onto an automated pipeline; the realistic equivalent is a GitHub Action that runs tests on push to main and reports failures, with gating enforced as a process rule rather than a technical block.

I want to scope this carefully: build a test suite and Action that reports pass/fail on push, but avoid recommending full auto-deploy CI/CD, since that would replace the manual "verify with real data in browser" discipline that's proven valuable all session for catching things automated tests miss (UI transitions, email delivery, visual regressions). Automated tests should supplement that manual verification, not replace it.

For test framework choice, Playwright fits the video's recommendation for web flows but would be heavier here given the server-rendered esbuild bundle + Express + SQLite setup requiring a full running stack in CI. For verifying internal calculation correctness like date math and dedup logic, simpler unit tests with Node's built-in test runner or vitest on the specific pure functions that have caused problems today would be lower-cost and higher-value to start with, saving Playwright end-to-end for a later phase.

I'm sketching a phased plan: Phase 1 prioritizes unit tests for the core pure logic functions that have caused issues.

For phase two, I'd add a handful of Playwright smoke tests for the most critical user flows like login, creating a wedding, sending automations, completing a public form, and signing a contract, focused on the paths that have broken most rather than full coverage.
